Also, a large proportion of articles lacked detailed descriptions of methodology and outcomes, participant selection, measurement, and confounding. Many had missing data. These issues contributed to > 20% of papers being classified as having an 'unclear' risk of bias. Other systematic reviews of non-randomized evidence in the Caribbean have also reported large proportions with a high risk of bias (14, 48). This speaks to the quality of reporting in the region and the necessity for establishing and adopting reporting standards to improve output.
